blocks.body:
A circle ties together distant parts of a figure. All points on one arc see a chord under the same angle; and if you draw any line through a fixed point $P$, the two pieces into which the circle cuts it have a constant product. These two facts, inscribed angles and the power of a point, are behind most problems involving circles, and lead to radical axes for several circles.

We use the notation and basic facts of [[euclid-basics]]: angle sums, similar triangles and the law of sines. Throughout, $\omega$ is a circle with centre $O$ and radius $r$.

blocks.title: Inscribed angles
blocks.body: A chord $BC$ splits $\omega$ into two arcs. For a point $A$ of $\omega$ other than $B$ and $C$, the angle $\angle BAC$ is called an inscribed angle; it stands on the arc $BC$ that does not contain $A$. The central angle on that arc is the angle at $O$ that the arc subtends; it exceeds $180^\circ$ if the arc is more than a semicircle. The basic theorem says that the inscribed angle depends only on the arc, not on where $A$ sits.

blocks.title: Inscribed angle theorem
blocks.body:
An inscribed angle is half the central angle standing on the same arc. Consequently:

1. All inscribed angles standing on the same arc are equal. In particular, if $A, B, C, D$ lie on $\omega$ with $B$ and $C$ on the same side of line $AD$, then $\angle ABD = \angle ACD$.
2. (Thales) An angle standing on a semicircle is a right angle.
3. If $A$ and $C$ lie on different arcs determined by $B$ and $D$, then $\angle BAD + \angle BCD = 180^\circ$.

First suppose that the centre $O$ lies on one arm of the angle, say on $AB$, so that $AB$ is a diameter. Triangle $OAC$ is isosceles with $OA = OC$, so $\angle OCA = \angle OAC$, and the exterior angle of this triangle at $O$ is $\angle BOC = \angle OAC + \angle OCA = 2\angle BAC$.

In general, draw the diameter $AA'$. Each of $\angle BAA'$ and $\angle A'AC$ has the centre on one arm, so the first case gives $\angle BOA' = 2\angle BAA'$ and $\angle A'OC = 2\angle A'AC$. If $O$ lies inside the angle $BAC$, add these: the arcs $BA'$ and $A'C$ together make up the arc $BC$ on which $\angle BAC$ stands. If $O$ lies outside, say with ray $AB$ between rays $AA'$ and $AC$, subtract instead: $\angle BAC = \angle A'AC - \angle A'AB$, and the arc $BC$ is the arc $A'C$ minus the arc $A'B$. Either way the central angle is twice the inscribed one.

For the consequences: in 1 both angles are half of the same central angle; in 2 the central angle is $180^\circ$; in 3 the two arcs $BD$ make up the whole circle, so the two central angles add up to $360^\circ$ and the two inscribed angles to $180^\circ$.

blocks.title: Cyclic quadrilaterals
blocks.body: A convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ is cyclic (its four vertices lie on one circle) if and only if $\angle A + \angle C = 180^\circ$. It is also cyclic if and only if $\angle ABD = \angle ACD$.

If $ABCD$ is convex and cyclic, its vertices occur around the circle in the order $A, B, C, D$, so $A$ and $C$ lie on different arcs determined by $B$ and $D$, and $\angle A + \angle C = 180^\circ$ by part 3 of the inscribed angle theorem.

Conversely, suppose $\angle A + \angle C = 180^\circ$, and let $\omega$ be the circle through $A$, $B$, $D$. The diagonals of a convex quadrilateral cross, at a point $E$ strictly between $B$ and $D$, and such a point lies inside $\omega$. So the ray from $A$ through $E$ leaves $\omega$ at a single point $C'$ beyond $E$, and $ABC'D$ is a convex cyclic quadrilateral with $\angle BC'D = 180^\circ - \angle A = \angle BCD$.

Both $C$ and $C'$ lie on the ray from $E$ pointing away from $A$. Suppose $C \ne C'$, say $C$ strictly between $E$ and $C'$ (the other case is the same with the roles exchanged). The ray $CE$ splits the angle $BCD$, so $\angle BCD = \angle BCE + \angle ECD$, and similarly $\angle BC'D = \angle BC'E + \angle EC'D$. In triangle $BCC'$ the angle $\angle BCE$ is the exterior angle at $C$, so it exceeds the interior angle $\angle BC'C = \angle BC'E$. Likewise $\angle ECD > \angle EC'D$. Adding, $\angle BCD > \angle BC'D$, a contradiction. So $C = C'$ lies on $\omega$.

The criterion $\angle ABD = \angle ACD$ is proved in the same way, using part 1 of the inscribed angle theorem in place of part 3.

blocks.title: Tangents
blocks.body:
A line through a point $T$ of $\omega$ is tangent there exactly when it is perpendicular to the radius $OT$; it then meets $\omega$ only at $T$. From a point $P$ outside $\omega$ there are two tangents, touching at $T_1$ and $T_2$, and $PT_1 = PT_2$, because the right triangles $OPT_1$ and $OPT_2$ share the hypotenuse $OP$ and have $OT_1 = OT_2$ (RHS).

A tangent behaves like a chord whose two endpoints have merged, and inscribed angles have a tangent version. Let $TB$ be a chord and $TS$ a ray along the tangent at $T$. Then the angle $\angle STB$ equals the inscribed angle $\angle TXB$ for every point $X$ of $\omega$ on the other side of line $TB$ from $S$. To see it, let $TT'$ be a diameter and choose $S$ on the same side of line $TT'$ as $B$. Since $TS \perp TT'$, we get $\angle STB = 90^\circ - \angle BTT'$, and in triangle $TBT'$, which has a right angle at $B$ by Thales, this equals $\angle TT'B$. That is an inscribed angle of the required kind, with $X = T'$, and all such inscribed angles are equal.

blocks.title: Power of a point
blocks.body:
The power of a point $P$ with respect to the circle $\omega$ (centre $O$, radius $r$) is
$$\operatorname{pow}(P) = PO^2 - r^2.$$
It is positive for $P$ outside $\omega$, zero on $\omega$ and negative inside; for $P$ outside it is the square of the length of the tangent from $P$.

blocks.title: Power of a point theorem
blocks.body:
Let a line through $P$ meet $\omega$ at $A$ and $B$, with $A = B$ if the line is tangent. Then
$$PA\cdot PB = |PO^2 - r^2|.$$
With signed lengths along the line, counting the product as positive when $A$ and $B$ are on the same side of $P$ and negative when $P$ lies between them, $PA \cdot PB = PO^2 - r^2$ exactly. In particular the product is the same for every line through $P$.

Let $M$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $O$ to the line. Since $OA = OB$, $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$. Put $h = OM$ and $t = MA = MB$. Pythagoras in triangles $OMA$ and $OMP$ gives $t^2 = r^2 - h^2$ and $PM^2 = PO^2 - h^2$.

If $P$ is on the line but outside the segment $AB$, the distances $PA$ and $PB$ are $PM - t$ and $PM + t$, so $PA\cdot PB = PM^2 - t^2 = PO^2 - r^2$, which is then non-negative. If $P$ lies between $A$ and $B$, they are $t - PM$ and $t + PM$, so $PA\cdot PB = t^2 - PM^2 = r^2 - PO^2$, and $P$ is inside $\omega$. With the sign convention the signed product is $PO^2 - r^2$ in both cases. For a tangent, $t = 0$ and $A = B = M$, so $PA^2 = PO^2 - r^2$.

The familiar special cases are: two chords $AB$ and $CD$ crossing at $P$ give $PA\cdot PB = PC\cdot PD$; two secants from an outside point give the same equation; a tangent $PT$ and a secant give $PT^2 = PA\cdot PB$.

The converse is also true and very useful: if lines $AB$ and $CD$ meet at $P$ and $PA\cdot PB = PC\cdot PD$ as signed products, then $A, B, C, D$ are concyclic. For crossing chords, say: the equation gives $PA/PD = PC/PB$, and the angles at $P$ are vertical angles, so triangles $PAC$ and $PDB$ are similar (SAS) and $\angle BAC = \angle BDC$. The points $A$ and $D$ lie on the same side of line $BC$, since $ACBD$ is a convex quadrilateral whose diagonals $AB$ and $CD$ cross at $P$, so the cyclic criterion applies.

blocks.title: Computing with power
blocks.body:
(a) Chords $AB$ and $CD$ of a circle of radius $7$ meet at $P$, with $PA = 3$, $PB = 8$, $PC = 4$. Find $PD$ and the distance from $P$ to the centre.

(b) A point $P$ is at distance $13$ from the centre of a circle of radius $5$. Find the length of the tangent from $P$, and check it on the secant through the centre.
blocks.solution:
(a) $PC\cdot PD = PA\cdot PB = 24$, so $PD = 6$. The power of $P$ is $-24$, so $PO^2 = r^2 - 24 = 49 - 24 = 25$ and $PO = 5$.

(b) The power of $P$ is $13^2 - 5^2 = 144$, so the tangent has length $12$; the tangent, the radius to the point of contact and $OP$ form a $5$-$12$-$13$ right triangle. The secant through the centre meets the circle at distances $13 - 5 = 8$ and $13 + 5 = 18$ from $P$, and indeed $8 \cdot 18 = 144 = 12^2$.

blocks.title: Radical axis and radical centre
blocks.body:
Take two circles $\omega_1, \omega_2$ with different centres. Which points have the same power with respect to both? The circle with centre $(p, q)$ and radius $r$ gives
$$\operatorname{pow}(x, y) = (x - p)^2 + (y - q)^2 - r^2 = x^2 + y^2 - 2px - 2qy + (p^2 + q^2 - r^2).$$
In the difference $\operatorname{pow}_1 - \operatorname{pow}_2$ the terms $x^2 + y^2$ cancel, leaving $2(p_2 - p_1)x + 2(q_2 - q_1)y + \text{const}$, a genuine linear expression because the centres differ. So the points of equal power form a line, perpendicular to the line of centres: the radical axis of the two circles. If the circles meet at $X$ and $Y$, both points have power $0$ with respect to both circles, so the radical axis is the line $XY$.

For three circles whose centres are not collinear, the three radical axes pass through one point, the radical centre. The axes of $\omega_1, \omega_2$ and of $\omega_2, \omega_3$ are perpendicular to the non-parallel lines $O_1O_2$ and $O_2O_3$, so they meet; their common point has equal power with respect to all three circles, so it lies on the third axis as well. This is often the quickest proof that three lines are concurrent.

blocks.title: A radical axis in coordinates
blocks.body: Find the radical axis of the circles $x^2 + y^2 = 4$ and $(x - 4)^2 + y^2 = 1$, and check that the tangents from a point on it to the two circles have equal length.
blocks.solution:
Setting $x^2 + y^2 - 4 = (x-4)^2 + y^2 - 1$ gives $-4 = -8x + 15$, so the radical axis is the line $x = \frac{19}{8}$, perpendicular to the line of centres (the $x$-axis). The circles do not meet, since $2 + 1 < 4$, but the axis still exists and lies between them.

From the point $(\frac{19}8, 0)$ the squared tangent lengths are
$$\left(\tfrac{19}8\right)^2 - 4 = \tfrac{361 - 256}{64} = \tfrac{105}{64} \qquad\text{and}\qquad \left(\tfrac{19}{8} - 4\right)^2 - 1 = \tfrac{169}{64} - 1 = \tfrac{105}{64},$$
equal as expected.

blocks.title: The radical axis bisects a common tangent
blocks.body: Two circles meet at $X$ and $Y$. A common tangent touches the first circle at $S$ and the second at $T$. Prove that line $XY$ passes through the midpoint of $ST$.
blocks.solution: Let $M$ be the midpoint of $ST$. The line $ST$ is tangent to the first circle at $S$, so the power of $M$ with respect to the first circle is $MS^2$. Likewise its power with respect to the second circle is $MT^2$. Since $MS = MT$, the point $M$ has equal powers, so it lies on the radical axis, which is the line $XY$.

blocks.title: Products along the altitudes
blocks.body: In an acute triangle $ABC$ the altitudes $AD$, $BE$, $CF$ meet at $H$. Prove that $HA\cdot HD = HB\cdot HE = HC\cdot HF$.
blocks.solution:
Since $\angle ADB = \angle AEB = 90^\circ$, both $D$ and $E$ lie on the circle with diameter $AB$. (This is the converse of Thales: in a right triangle the midpoint of the hypotenuse is equidistant from all three vertices.) In this circle, $AD$ and $BE$ are chords, and they cross at $H$, which lies inside the acute triangle and hence strictly inside both chords. By the power of the point $H$, $HA\cdot HD = HB\cdot HE$. The same argument with the circle on diameter $BC$ gives $HB\cdot HE = HC\cdot HF$.

The common value is minus the power of $H$ with respect to the circles on the sides as diameters; see [[triangle-centres]].

blocks.body:
- The criterion $\angle A + \angle C = 180^\circ$ is for a convex quadrilateral with vertices in the order $A, B, C, D$. If four concyclic points lie around the circle in the order $A, B, D, C$, then $ABCD$ is self-intersecting and the criterion fails; use $\angle ABD = \angle ACD$ instead.
- Equal angles $\angle ABD = \angle ACD$ prove concyclicity only if $B$ and $C$ are on the same side of line $AD$.
- The tangent-chord angle equals the inscribed angle from the other side of the chord, not from the same side.
- Concentric circles have no radical axis, and for three circles with collinear centres the radical axes are parallel or coincide instead of meeting.

Power of a point is the bridge to [[geo-transformations]]: for $P$ outside $\omega$, the inversion with centre $P$ and radius squared $\operatorname{pow}(P)$ maps $\omega$ onto itself, and many inversion arguments begin with a power computation. The circumcircle, incircle and nine-point circle of [[triangle-centres]] are handled with these tools. With vectors, the signed product is the dot product $(A - P)\cdot(B - P)$ ([[vectors-plane]], [[analytic-geometry]]). Chord lengths $2r\sin\theta$ connect circles with [[trig]], and Ptolemy's inequality belongs to [[geo-inequalities]].

1. Chords $AB$ and $CD$ of a circle meet at an interior point $P$, with $PA = 2$, $PB = 6$ and $CD = 7$. Find $PC$ and $PD$.
2. The tangent at $A$ to the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ (with $AB \ne AC$) meets line $BC$ at $T$. Prove that $TB/TC = (AB/AC)^2$.
3. Prove that if two circles are tangent at a point, their radical axis is the common tangent line at that point.
4. A convex cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ has perpendicular diagonals meeting at $P$. Prove that the line through $P$ perpendicular to $AB$ passes through the midpoint of $CD$.
